messages.subject: L-BFGS
messages.body_plain:
Quick question for everyone.  I'm considering implementing the limited memory version of BFGS in Stan.  The question is whether we would prefer this as a "new" algorithm (i.e., the users could set algorithm=bfgs or algorithm=lbfgs (or maybe algorithm=bfgs hessian_approx=limited) or simply as a drop-in replacement for BFGS.

The argument for the drop-in replacement is that, honestly, there's not a lot of reason to use BFGS if L-BFGS is available.  In general L-BFGS works better than BFGS and uses *much* less memory.  The flip side is that it's easy enough to have both just in case someone wanted to use BFGS instead.

I realize that most people may not care about this, but I thought I would check in before I got started.  Thoughts?

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
Nocedal and Wright

http://download.springer.com.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/static/pdf/264/chp%253A10.1007%252F978-0-387-40065-5_7.pdf?auth66=1383700937_ddec5bba9ea5a1994ae00038b73a436a&ext=.pdf

claims on page 180 that "The main weakness of the L-BFGS method is that it converges slowly on ill-conditioned problems—specifically, on problems where the Hessian matrix contains a wide distribution of eigenvalues." This is basically the same deal as strong Wolfe vs. weak Wolfe: I don't know how we can presume that the user has a well-conditioned / non-degenerate / etc. problem, particularly if someone is using it for some arbitrary optimization problem as opposed to finding a posterior mode or whatever.

So, I think we should have options. The documentation of L-BFGS is basically the same as the documentation of BFGS with about 1 additional option.

Ben

> well-conditioned / non-degenerate / etc. problem, particularly if someone is using it for some arbitrary optimization
> problem as opposed to finding a posterior mode or whatever.

Is BFGS better behaved?  I didn't see a direct comparison.
In fact, I can't seem to find much practical discussion anywhere
of plain-old BFGS.

Also, given that we're doing positive-definite Hessian
approximations, is there some connection to what we'll be
doing with Michael's SoftAbs construction for RHMC?

> So, I think we should have options. The documentation of L-BFGS is basically the same as the documentation of BFGS with
> about 1 additional option.

The effort's not in the original doc or even in the initial
coding, but in the maintenance.

And by that, I mean not only the doc, but also testing of
the algorithm and its interfaces through to command/R/Python,
as well as dealing with questions on the mailing list.

And again, these aren't just write once and they work forever,
any refactoring requires more work again because of the two alternatives.

If BFGS and L-BFGS have different behavior in terms of convergence
or efficiency, we need to doc it so that users know which one to
use.  If one dominates the other, we only need the good one.

I'm not saying we shouldn't have both --- I don't know much
about either.  I'm just trying to point out that multiplying
options is by no means cheap in software we plan to maintain.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: L-BFGS
messages.body_plain:
I don't think L-BFGS dominates BFGS or vice versa, even within a particular class of optimization problems. Also, you wouldn't necessarily know if the Hessian were ill-conditioned until you solve the problem. In the chapter on limited memory methods, Nocedal and Wright are only comparing L-BFGS to other limited memory methods. I don't remember them ever comparing L-BFGS to BFGS because the main difference between them is that L-BFGS is simply necessary when your optimization problem has so many parameters that the machine doesn't have enough RAM to do BFGS.

But in the BFGS chapter

http://download.springer.com.ezproxy.cul.columbia.edu/static/pdf/265/chp%253A10.1007%252F978-0-387-40065-5_6.pdf?auth66=1383747383_b6da37dfd810ad1d77e52760cb0ffce8&ext=.pdf

they do talk about the ability of BFGS to self-correct within a few iterations if the Hessian approximation strays. Also, at some point during the process, BFGS achieves better than linear convergence on well-behaved problems, whereas I think L-BFGS is linear throughout.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: L-BFGS
messages.body_plain:
My memory is fuzzy, but I recall seeing comparisons between BFGS and L-BFGS suggesting that, while L-BFGS has a slower theoretical rate of convergence, in practice it can actually converge a little faster, particularly when the curvature of the space varies significantly.  I can't find the paper anymore, but I think this was based on results on the CUTE test problems.  Anyway, I think I will implement both for now.  In fact, it should be straightforward to simply include L-BFGS as an option when running BFGS.  As part of it I'd like to include some tests on the models and we could use that to potentially make a final decision.

Regarding the Newton method, I know I've suggested removing it for the mean time.  The reason isn't so much that the optimization method is bad, but that it's currently computing the Hessian using a finite difference which will be, at best, inefficient.  Once we have higher-order autodiff and the Newton method uses that to get the Hessian, then it's definitely worth having for small to medium sized problems.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.body_plain:
I think we need to talk about granularity in these issues
and whether we need a finer-grained plan of attack as
part of the issues.

Ensemble samplers also require work on the convergence
monitoring --- wasn't that the main holdup?  And also on
initialization.  They'll require changing the command-line
interfaces, too.

There are two families of such algorithms:

   * differential evolution and DREAM
   * Goodman and Weare's walk and stretch moves

- Bob

P.S.  Another, separate issue is adaptation that communicates
       across chains.

See the email I just sent out.  Algorithms like this ideally being as generic ideas and
then are reduced to a list of dependencies and implementations which define a plan
of attack before any dev effort is made.

> Ensemble samplers also require work on the convergence
> monitoring --- wasn't that the main holdup?  And also on
> initialization.  They'll require changing the command-line
> interfaces, too.
>
> There are two families of such algorithms:
>
>  * differential evolution and DREAM
>  * Goodman and Weare's walk and stretch moves
>
> - Bob
>
> P.S.  Another, separate issue is adaptation that communicates
>      across chains.

The way I picture it is first extending the sampler architecture to handle an ensemble of samplers
be default (with an ensemble of one reproducing the current behavior).   Then we define
ensemble I/O (initialization, output averaging, etc), argument configuration, and then
we'd be able to implement all kinds of ensemble methods quickly (not to mention communicating
adaptation).

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Re: L-BFGS
messages.body_plain:
It's hard to say anything about the relative speeds of the two
algorithms during search. During convergence, BFGS achieves
superlinear convergence whereas LBFGS only achieves linear
convergence. That is, roughly speaking, –log(distance from optimum)
increases superlinearly with BFGS, whereas it only increases linearly
with LBFGS (same as gradient descent, but with better constants). In
practical terms, this means that if you use BFGS you might as well
wait for it to converge fully (modulo early stopping-type concerns),
whereas you might be waiting a very long time for LBFGS to converge to
10 digits of accuracy or whatever.

Matt

> curvature of the space varies significantly.  I can't find the paper
> anymore, but I think this was based on results on the CUTE test problems.
> Anyway, I think I will implement both for now.  In fact, it should be
> straightforward to simply include L-BFGS as an option when running BFGS.  As
> part of it I'd like to include some tests on the models and we could use
> that to potentially make a final decision.

> Regarding the Newton method, I know I've suggested removing it for the mean
> time.  The reason isn't so much that the optimization method is bad, but
> that it's currently computing the Hessian using a finite difference which
> will be, at best, inefficient.  Once we have higher-order autodiff and the

messages.subject: Shuffling in make/tests: unsafe?
messages.body_plain:
Ben,

It looks like the call to RScript can kill the whole build process if a user has a custom Rprofile. Is it possible to not do anything custom or silence that from the call to Rscript?

Maybe it's time to rethink the shuffling strategy. Do we actually need all these dependencies?
- where
- which
- shuf
- Rscript
- python
- perl
Perhaps we can go back to the default, alphabetical order or hard-code a dependency list. It's making me nervous that calling Rscript can inject things into the makefile that stops a user from building Stan.

Daniel

>> convergence. That is, roughly speaking, –log(distance from optimum)
>> increases superlinearly with BFGS, whereas it only increases linearly
>> with LBFGS (same as gradient descent, but with better constants). In
>> practical terms, this means that if you use BFGS you might as well
>> wait for it to converge fully (modulo early stopping-type concerns),

>>> anymore, but I think this was based on results on the CUTE test problems.
>>> Anyway, I think I will implement both for now.  In fact, it should be
>>> straightforward to simply include L-BFGS as an option when running BFGS.  As
>>> part of it I'd like to include some tests on the models and we could use
>>> that to potentially make a final decision.
>>>

>>> time.  The reason isn't so much that the optimization method is bad, but
>>> that it's currently computing the Hessian using a finite difference which
>>> will be, at best, inefficient.  Once we have higher-order autodiff and the
>>> Newton method uses that to get the Hessian, then it's definitely worth
>>> having for small to medium sized problems.
>>>
>>> Cheers,
>>> Marcus
>>>
>>>
>>>
>>> On Mon, Nov 4, 2013 at 12:13 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

messages.subject: Re: Shuffling in make/tests: unsafe?
messages.body_plain:
I said it already on github but I think we can just add --vanilla to the Rscript invocation to avoid the custom Rprofile problem. That is what we had to do with RStan.

Ben

> - where
> - which
> - shuf
> - Rscript

messages.subject: B-Splines
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I've started work on implementing B-splines in Stan. With Bob's help I've been able to write a function bspline function that is "working" (i.e. agrees with other results but isn't completely tested). This lets me write things in the model/transformed parameters blocks like

ymean[i] <- bspline(P, x[i], beta, knots);

to assign ymean[i] the value of an order P B-spline curve evaluated at x with coefficients beta and knot vector knots. I've attached my first pass at this function.

Since I'm not terribly familiar with Stan's internals I have some implementation questions:

1) How do I check that the knots are ordered and distinct? Is there an appropriate stan::math::validate function or something?

2) If x and the knots are given as data, the correct thing to do is not to use the function above but to precompute a design matrix a la bs() in R. Of course users could do this in R, but it would be nice to have something like

W <- bspline_design(P, X, knots);

in the transformed parameters block and this is straightforward to implement. However, that W matrix is very sparse - at any x there are at most P nonzero basis functions in the B-spline expansion. So If the knot vector is long then it might be worthwhile to just store the P nonzero basis functions and an integer index into the knot/beta vectors. On a long shot, is there an existing data structure for something like that? Or are Eigen's sparse vectors coming?

3) My original need for this functionality came from a project where I have missing x's and varying knots. I got this working in the transformed parameters block using the same method as in the attached header file (this is the standard method for computing B splines).

But I suspect I'm hosing part of the gradient when I find x's location in the knot vector - is that true? There are other ways to compute B splines that might not have the same problem, although they are less efficient. In any event, I can compute the gradient myself; in x it's an order P-1 B-spline, and the in the knots it's another B spline as well, and I'm hoping to implement that at some point too. Of course, 2) is much more straightforward, and probably the most useful to the largest number of people.

messages.body_plain:
On 11/8/13, 3:08 PM, Marcus Brubaker wrote:
> Agreed, in theory there is little to be said about search.  I am basing my assessment on empirical results on a number
> of test problems.  I'm not sure which paper I'm remembering, but poking around turned up
> http://www.ece.northwestern.edu/~nocedal/PDFfiles/limited-memory.pdf (see table 4 on page 8).  I wish I could find the
> 1988 tech report they reference, as it seems likely to have more results.
>
> Ben, thanks for posting a list of the problems having issues with optimization.  I'll take a look and see what's
> happening with them.

We know some of them aren't going to work in practice
because there are no modes.

If it's possible and not too much work, it'd be great to diagnose that
in the same way that the sampler diagnoses an improper posterior.

And by the way, Daniel and I have been using the optimizer
for the diff-eq models we've been developing and it's awesome.
The sampler takes about 10 minutes times 4 chains to generate 100
or so effective samples using the non-hierarchial model, whereas
the optimizer runs in about 30 seconds.  This is just auto-diffing
a non-stiff integrator so far.

- Bob

It should be possible.  Basically, if it stops optimizing due to a small change in objective value or small move in parameter space and the gradient is still large it probably means the function is unbounded and has no mode.  (It could also be a bug, an error in the gradient or an objective with extremely bad curvature, but those are less likely.)

Marcus

Thoughts on the models I've looked at so far:

- schools is known to not have a mode (there was a bug about that a few weeks ago)
- I just tested inhalers and lsat and both ran as I would have expected.  lsat looks like it might have found a large plateau, so may not be finding the optima, but that's just a limitation of quasi-Newton methods
- salm looks like random inits are putting it in such a bad spot that no decent step can be found.  (The initial log prob tends to eb around -1e189, which is clearly bad.)  Running with init=0 is fine though.

salm should be bailing out instead of looping with those bad inits.  I'll look into what's going on there when I get a chance.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.subject: Re: B-Splines
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jared, On Friday, November 8, 2013 1:02:38 PM UTC-5, Jared Murray wrote: > Hello all, > > I've started work on implementing B-splines in Stan. With Bob's help I've been able to write a function bspline function that is "working" (i.e. agrees with other results but isn't completely tested). This lets me write things in the model/transformed parameters blocks like > > ymean[i] <- bspline(P, x[i], beta, knots); > > to assign ymean[i] the value of an order P B-spline curve evaluated at x with coefficients beta and knot vector knots. I've attached my first pass at this function. Thanks for contributing to Stan! > Since I'm not terribly familiar with Stan's internals I have some implementation questions: > > 1) How do I check that the knots are ordered and distinct? Is there an appropriate stan::math::validate function or something? See goodrich@CYBERPOWERPC:/opt/stan$ git grep -F "check_ordered" src/ | cat src/stan/io/reader.hpp: *

See stan::math::check_ordered(T) for src/stan/io/reader.hpp: stan::math::check_ordered("stan::io::ordered(%1%)", x, "Constrained vector"); src/stan/io/writer.hpp: stan::math::check_ordered("stan::io::ordered_unconstrain(%1%)", y, "Vector"); src/stan/math/error_handling/matrix/check_ordered.hpp: bool check_ordered(const char* function, src/stan/math/error_handling/matrix/check_ordered.hpp: bool check_ordered(const char* function, src/stan/math/error_handling/matrix/check_ordered.hpp: return check_ordered(function,y,name,result); src/stan/math/matrix_error_handling.hpp:#include src/stan/prob/transform.hpp: stan::math::check_ordered("stan::prob::ordered_free(%1%)", src/test/math/error_handling/matrix/check_ordered_test.cpp:#include > 2) If x and the knots are given as data, the correct thing to do is not to use the function above but to precompute a design matrix a la bs() in R. Of course users could do this in R, but it would be nice to have something like > > W <- bspline_design(P, X, knots); > > in the transformed parameters block and this is straightforward to implement. However, that W matrix is very sparse - at any x there are at most P nonzero basis functions in the B-spline expansion. So If the knot vector is long then it might be worthwhile to just store the P nonzero basis functions and an integer index into the knot/beta vectors. On a long shot, is there an existing data structure for something like that? Or are Eigen's sparse vectors coming? There are no sparse operations now and it could easily be years before anything like that is implemented. I think if Stan multiplies something by a zero constant, it at least knows not to add to the auto-diff tree. You could write a function that inputs such a W and returns a ymean vector where you could internally do some tricks to speed up the computation. That is probably third or fourth order though. > 3) My original need for this functionality came from a project where I have missing x's and varying knots. I got this working in the transformed parameters block using the same method as in the attached header file (this is the standard method for computing B splines). > > But I suspect I'm hosing part of the gradient when I find x's location in the knot vector - is that true? There are other ways to compute B splines that might not have the same problem, although they are less efficient. In any event, I can compute the gradient myself; in x it's an order P-1 B-spline, and the in the knots it's another B spline as well, and I'm hoping to implement that at some point too. Of course, 2) is much more straightforward, and probably the most useful to the largest number of people. As far as I can tell, you are not misleading the auto-differ, although you can try your model in test gradient mode to compare with numeric derivatives. Do you have a reference for this way of handling missing covariates? In any event, being able to do parts of the gradient analytically can lead to a nice boost in performance. Ben

messages.body_plain:
A good way to test the auto-diff is with finite
differences on the double-based version of the
function.  There are various examples in the code now
that do finite difference tests.  I'm about to abstract
the finite difference operation using functionals
on functors, so not every test needs to reimplement
finite diffs.

For (2), there are various ways to implement sparse
and/or ragged structures.  For example, a sparse
matrix A can be set up parallel arrays

   int r[N];
   int c[N];
   real v[N];

so that

   v[n] == A[r[n], c[n]]

There are, unfortunately, no built-in ways to manipulate
such structures using matrix ops.  Ben's right about
it not being at the top of our priority list.

Great projects for someone to take on would be sparse
matrices and ragged arrays.

The dropping rules for terms are pretty sparse, and at the
moment, we don't drop terms that are multiplied by zero.  Maybe
we should be doing that --- it depends how common it is going to be.
We do drop 0 under addition and 1 under multiplication.

- Bob

messages.subject: onions
messages.body_plain:
The attached .stan file implements yet another way to draw a correlation matrix from the LKJ distribution. It works well if you call it from R with

onion <- stan(file = "onion.stan", model_name = "onion", data = list(K = 4, eta = 1))

But if you move the model block to the end of the file and rename the generated quantities block to transformed parameters, then it fails to initialize after 100 attempts and aborts with the "No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?" statement. This does not make sense because the implied correlation matrix created in transformed parameters is not even used and the primitive parameters are just standard normals and betas. So, I think something else is going on, but it is not spitting out any useful messages.

Ben

messages.subject: new web site
messages.body_plain:
I redesigned the web site for Stan over the weekend.

You can find it at:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/webpages

The actual site is all linked from:

    mc-stan.org/index.html <http://mc-stan.org/index.html>

Of course, we have the ultimate "bike shed issue" now:

   What color should the web site be?

I'm sort of partial to the pistachio I went with, but
am not wedded to it.

Any other style and content suggestions welcome.

One issue I have given that we list the development team
is where we should draw the line in terms of contribution.
I added Allen Riddell, who's making ongoing contributions
for PyStan.  Should I add a section for people who've done
significant work on one piece of Stan, like Rob Goedman's
refactoring of the parser?  I'm trying to take care of at
least thanking everyone in the manual.

- Bob

messages.subject: PNaCL
messages.body_plain:
Now that it is finally officially released (to developers), I think Stan should pursue PNaCL

http://blog.chromium.org/2013/11/portable-native-client-pinnacle-of.html

In short, this is a Google effort that lets you use a LLVM-based compiler to create the intermediate representation of binary-ish code and then Chrome the webbrowser can execute it (in a sandbox) on the major platforms without the end-user having to compile anything or losing much speed. There is also an API for accessing local data files.

I was thinking about using this or emscripten for the missing data thing if IES approves my grant proposal, but I think it would be good for Stan generally. People could distribute (or host) Stan models this way and http://mc-stan.org could live-demonstrate all of Stan's examples (in whatever color scheme).

What we need is some 12 year old HTML5 speaking little dude to write an app that would provide a high-level interface to calling an arbitrary Stan model (and then print samples*.csv), like what we do with RStan and PyStan except more GUI-ish for the web-based user. If we could find a guy like that (wouldn't need to know stats), then that effort could proceed in parallel to the rest of the stuff we are doing and wouldn't be all that difficult to maintain going forward since it would basically just be calling command-line Stan within a browser.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I can't retain a bcc, but I trust that Bob can reforward (although I did not mean to imply that Mitzi would be a 12 year old HTML5 speaking little dude). It is a one-time semi-compile to an intermediate representation and then Chrome can execute from the intermediate representation on any prevalent platform. You can use optimization when building and it is something like a 5% slowdown relative to native on average for the projects that have been tested (they are mostly targeting games, so who knows about stat computing). Last time I checked (a few months ago), test-unit was passing with their forked llvm / clang semi-compiler; Google definitely intends that you not have to make (m)any changes to your codebase.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
I was trying to code review Marcus's pull request:

   https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/pull/346/files

but got very confused by all the pointers flying around
in the very first file I looked at:

https://github.com/mbrubake/stan/blob/3d3b350cc407ea4feb5855ba853744c35d7a65ae/src/stan/agrad/rev/matrix/ldlt.hpp

For example, in LDLT_factor, there's a new in the second
constructor but there's no destructor in which it's freed.
Is that because it's going on the auto-diff memory alloc?

In mdivide_left_ldlt_alloc, it looks like there's a different
approach to memory management with a

   boost::shared_ptr< Eigen::LDLT< Eigen::Matrix<double,R1,C1> > > _ldltP;

Maybe somebody else could review this code?

I'd rather not see code from different name spaces in the
same file.  This ldlt.hpp file defines entries for stan::math
and stan::agrad.  The point was that there shouldn't be any
dependency from math to agrad, so we could compile math separately.
We can't really do that if we mix stan::agrad and stan::math
definitions in a single file.

Given that we have outstanding bugs that already seem to be
malloc related, I'd like to be very careful before introduing
more pointer manipulation that isn't fully encapsulated.

- Bob

The intent of gitflow is basically that a critical bugfix goes into a hotfix branch (and gets merged into develop) while noncritical bugs are fixed in develop only. Basically, hotfix branches have approximately one commit and there is a new release as soon as it is verified that the patch actually fixes the bug.

I think that is fine in general. I was just saying that if you have already branched from develop (whether that was appropriate in retrospect or not), it is probably better to make a normal release from that branch, as opposed to trying to cherry-pick parts of it onto a branch off master.

Ben

messages.subject: pointers and casts in command.hpp
messages.body_plain:
Now I'm looking at the code for command.hpp in the
current develop branch and see this:

     template<class Sampler>
     bool init_adapt(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler, categorical_argument* adapt) {

       ... snip ...

       Sampler* s = dynamic_cast<Sampler*>(sampler);

Why wasn't this written to use argument inference as:

   template <class Sampler>
   bool
   init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, ...

and then you don't need the dynamic cast.  Or any cast.
And could it be declared const?

Same function, but now in the ...snip... part there's this:

       double delta = dynamic_cast<real_argument*>(adapt->arg("delta"))->value();

Why is there a cast here?  The problem with doing this this way
is that there's no compile-time guarantee of types.

Would there be a way to overload the arg method in adapt, and do something
like this:

     init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, const categorical_argument& adapt) {
         ...
         double delta = adapt.get_double("delta");

This eliminates the cast and all that cut-and-paste of arrows and
asterisks and parens (this pattern shows up all over the command.hpp
file).

Although this guarantees all the types, presumably the get_double()
method would have to throw an exception if it represented a value
that's not a double value.

Overall, it's very dangerous to be calling these arguments by
a string-based name any way you slice it.  Even better would
be something like:

     double delta = adapt.get_delta();

that's guaranteed to be well-defined and return the right type
of value.  That then requires you to push more of the logic back
into the argument class.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I think that most people who use gitflow would not really accept the idea of doing a bugfix release whenever you want; rather you do a bugfix release whenever you have to. If none of the bugs rise to that level of severity, then I think it is fine to push the fixes into develop and then do a normal release whenever you want. The problem we had with 2.0 was that we couldn't do a normal release when we wanted to because a lot of big but interrelated stuff was being merged intermittently.

But if develop is in good shape now, then I don't think there is really anything wrong with treating the "hotfix" branch you made as a "release" branch.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pointers and casts in command.hpp
messages.body_plain:
> Now I'm looking at the code for command.hpp in the
> current develop branch and see this:
>
>    template<class Sampler>
>    bool init_adapt(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler, categorical_argument* adapt) {
>
>      ... snip ...
>
>      Sampler* s = dynamic_cast<Sampler*>(sampler);
>
>
> Why wasn't this written to use argument inference as:
>
>  template <class Sampler>
>  bool
>  init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, ...
>
> and then you don't need the dynamic cast.  Or any cast.
> And could it be declared const?

The only issue is that you have to template everything -- which would necessitate
touching not just command.hpp but also the mcmc_writer at the very least.

Your mutating the sampler directly -- won't that explicitly prevent the use of const?

> Same function, but now in the ...snip... part there's this:
>
>      double delta = dynamic_cast<real_argument*>(adapt->arg("delta"))->value();
>
> Why is there a cast here?  The problem with doing this this way
> is that there's no compile-time guarantee of types.

You have to cast because the arg tree is navigated based on the base,
virtual class definition (I don't see a way to do this that would still
allow the recursive navigation).  If you want to use an arg's derived behavior
after navigating then you have to cast back to the explicit class.

I don't disagree that there's no compile-time guarantee, but this code
is also not dynamic so there's no run-time case we haven't already
checked in the arg unit-tests.

>
> Would there be a way to overload the arg method in adapt, and do something
> like this:
>
>    init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, const categorical_argument& adapt) {
>        ...
>        double delta = adapt.get_double("delta");
>
> This eliminates the cast and all that cut-and-paste of arrows and
> asterisks and parens (this pattern shows up all over the command.hpp
> file).
>
> Although this guarantees all the types, presumably the get_double()
> method would have to throw an exception if it represented a value
> that's not a double value.
>
> Overall, it's very dangerous to be calling these arguments by
> a string-based name any way you slice it.  Even better would
> be something like:
>
>    double delta = adapt.get_delta();
>
> that's guaranteed to be well-defined and return the right type
> of value.  That then requires you to push more of the logic back
> into the argument class.

It's not just rearranging the logic -- it's completely changing the hierarchical
structure.  Adapt is essentially a container class, and has no concept
of what it contains outside of a bunch of derived arg classes.  In order
to write methods as you described above you would either have to
(a) hard code everything which would be a nightmare given the
combinatorics or (b) write get_double, get_string, etc for every container
class and then throw exceptions everywhere.  In either case you're
undercutting the utility of the polymorphism.

Again, in practice this isn't an issue because the arg unit-tests run
every argument configuration so that we know there are no run-time
conflicts.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] writing '\0' in command.hpp
messages.body_plain:
Make it an issue.  This is actually more expansive, as the behavior
here is meant to mirror the behavior in the arg code.  I originally
went with a single char to enforce the prefix being a single
character long, and '\0' is the closest thing to an empty char.
I'll change everything to strings and just allow prefixes of any size.

On Nov 14, 2013, at 2:53 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Sorry for not code reviewing this more the first time, but
> I'm continuing to look at command.hpp and see this:
>
>   void write_stan(std::ostream* s, const char prefix = '\0') {
>      if(!s) return;
>
>      *s << prefix << " stan_version_major = " << stan::MAJOR_VERSION << std::endl;
>      *s << prefix << " stan_version_minor = " << stan::MINOR_VERSION << std::endl;
>      *s << prefix << " stan_version_patch = " << stan::PATCH_VERSION << std::endl;
>
>    }
>
> You really don't want to be writing '\0' out.  It's the
> plain-old C string terminator character 0.
>
> Following advice from here:
>
>  http://stackoverflow.com/questions/14795565/difference-between-null-terminated-char-0-and
>
> I wrote this little C++ program:
>
>
>  #include <iostream>
>
>  int main() {
>    std::cout << '\0' << "abc" << std::endl;
>  }
>
> which produces this:
>
>  ~/temp2$ clang++ pound.cpp
>  ~/temp2$ ./a.out | hexdump -C
>  00000000  00 61 62 63 0a                                    |.abc.|
>  00000005
>
> You see the '\0' written out as the first hex value 00, then
> the "abc" as 61, 62, and 63, then the newline as 0a.
>
> If you just print without piping through hexdump, the '\0' disappears,
> but apparently that behavior isn't cross-platform.
>
> But the only time write_stan() gets called in our code base,
> it's called with prefix = '#'.  So why not default to '#' and
> then not include the '#' in the call?
>
> I think it's better to not try to guess at how to make functions
> like this flexible before we have a use for that flexibility.
>
> If you want configurable prefixes, use strings and default
> to the empty string.
>
>   void write_stan(std::ostream* s, const char* prefix = "") {
>      if (!s) return;
>      *s << prefix << "stan_version_major = " << stan::MAJOR_VERSION
>         << std::endl
>         << prefix << "stan_version_minor = " << stan::MINOR_VERSION
>         << std::endl
>         << prefix << "stan_version_patch = " << stan::PATCH_VERSION
>         << std::endl;
>    }
>
> and then call it with:
>
>   write_stan(s, "# ");
>
> You probably don't want to assume an initial space if there's not a prefix.
>
> - Bob
>
>

messages.body_plain:
> In fact, I'd be tempted to have the sampler class have a flag indicating
> whether to call that init_static thing so that it's part of sample, as in:
>
>  switch (sampler_select) {
>     case 0:
>       return sample(stan::mcmc::unit_e_static_hmc(model,base_rng),
>                     ...);
>
>
>  template <class S>
>  int sample(S& s, ...) {
>    if (s.requires_init_static())
>      if (!init_static_hmc<sampler>(s, algo))
>        return 0;
>    ... do something with s...
>    return 0;  // normal return
>  }
>
> You could probably just have something like s::requires_init_static
> as a static boolean class variable so you don't even need a method.

But then we'd have to have each sampler implementation be aware
of all other implementations through the possible initializations,
which break the encapsulation.  I do not like that.

> Also, should that return from the conditional on init_static_hmc
> failing be 0 or something indicating a failure to initialize?

I'd rather it fail with 0, because it means that command.hpp is not
configured correctly.  Remember all of these things get called
in unit-tests so they'd pop up in tests before we make them visible
to users.

> I'd be happy to go through and do the refactoring.

Just be aware that you'll have to hit other code that uses the
sampler pointers -- or at least you'll have to convert to pointers
at some place.  I don't think (pointer == 0) is used anywhere
so that shouldn't be a problem, but just in case.

> P.S.  I'd also much rather see the numerically obfuscated switch replaced
>      with an if-then structure.  But I can see how reasonable people would
>      differ on this preference.

I draw the line after two nested ifs, especially when they're repeated
this much.  An explicit if/then would be a nightmare to read, which is
why I went to a single switch with the built up index.

> P.P.S.  Why static_cast<int>(adapt_engaged);  Isn't adapt_engaged already
>        boolean?  You just want to be explicit?

Cast to an int for courtesy before being used in the integer arithmetic
that builds up the unique sampler index.

> P.P.P.S.  It's good style to declare variables close to where you define them.
>          The sampler_ptr was defined way before the case statement to set it
>          and not used in between.  But that'll be moot once we get rid of
>          the pointers.

That's an artifact of only having HMC samplers at the moment.  If we have
another sampler then it would have used the same sampler_ptr.

>
> But then we'd have to have each sampler implementation be aware
> of all other implementations through the possible initializations,
> which break the encapsulation.  I do not like that.

Agreed.  It's a tradeoff, like all coding.  You can either repeat
yourself in multiple places or try to make a generalization.  But
it's not worth doing if the generalization is forced.

>> Also, should that return from the conditional on init_static_hmc
>> failing be 0 or something indicating a failure to initialize?
>
> I'd rather it fail with 0, because it means that command.hpp is not
> configured correctly.

It that's the case, raise an exception and dump out a message.

The standard thing to do is to trust your code by unit testing,
not put in a run-time test.

> Remember all of these things get called
> in unit-tests so they'd pop up in tests before we make them visible
> to users.
>
>> I'd be happy to go through and do the refactoring.
>
> Just be aware that you'll have to hit other code that uses the
> sampler pointers -- or at least you'll have to convert to pointers
> at some place.  I don't think (pointer == 0) is used anywhere
> so that shouldn't be a problem, but just in case.

Of course.

>> P.S.  I'd also much rather see the numerically obfuscated switch replaced
>>       with an if-then structure.  But I can see how reasonable people would
>>       differ on this preference.
>
> I draw the line after two nested ifs, especially when they're repeated
> this much.  An explicit if/then would be a nightmare to read, which is
> why I went to a single switch with the built up index.

I very strongly disagree.

The way you have it requires lining up how the int gets constructed in
multiple loops via arithmetic and then lining up the resulting magic
numbers with the case statements.  The key to readability is having
local decisions made locally.

Luckily, Daniel's going to break this logjam of disagreement with
an even better suggestion --- we write little functions that
do the work for us so the code's both readable, encapsulated, and
has no magic numbers or deeply nested ifs.

I'll call that out in the next e-mail.  We'll deal with the refacroring
so you don't have to worry about it.

>> P.P.S.  Why static_cast<int>(adapt_engaged);  Isn't adapt_engaged already
>>         boolean?  You just want to be explicit?
>
> Cast to an int for courtesy before being used in the integer arithmetic
> that builds up the unique sampler index.

OK --- I'd rather just rely on how the compiler is specified to
work in these cases, but I'm not adamant about it.  Or, use
the logical nature of the boolean in a ternary/conditional operator.

>> P.P.P.S.  It's good style to declare variables close to where you define them.
>>           The sampler_ptr was defined way before the case statement to set it
>>           and not used in between.  But that'll be moot once we get rid of
>>           the pointers.
>
> That's an artifact of only having HMC samplers at the moment.  If we have
> another sampler then it would have used the same sampler_ptr.

Define a new one, then, or refactor the code.  Lingering variables
with multiple purposes is just hard to follow (a bad code "smell" as
the refactoring folks would have it).

I know it's Java and ten years plus old, but I'd highly recommend
Fowler's book "Refactoring".  It's all about writing code for readability
and maintainability.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] forward-looking transformations
messages.body_plain:
I am less hopeful on automated transformations.  The problem is that non-centered
parameterizations are not always the best approach (so you'll have to enable some
ability to turn any automated transformation on and off) and in many cases they
don't even make sense (anything beyond a one-level hierarchy).  Personally I don't
think locking users into building one-layer multilevel models is worth the possible
convenience.

>

>> So, we have a several examples of Matt-trickish things where the optimal thing to do would be to put a prior on
>> primitive parameters and transform them to imply a particular prior on substantive parameters. Currently, we are forcing
>> users to do all these tricks in the .stan file, which can be tedious and / or error prone.
>
> Agreed.
>
> > We could write convenience
>> functions to do the transformations (and maybe optimize the derivatives internally), but it would still be up to the
>> user to put the appropriate prior on the primitive parameters, which would still be tedious and error-prone.
>
> But in this case, those would be standardized and
> could get matching functions or it could all be rolled
> into a single function.
>
>> Is there some way we can design things so that particular transformation functions get to change the log-posterior? So,
>
> Yes, it's possible.  It's basically how the
> log probability functions.  The parser recognizes
> a function ending in "_log" (a very bad choice in
> retrospect) and adds an argument for lp__, which
> is passed by non-constant reference.
>
> Scope of where these functions are allowed is restricted
> to the blocks where there is a log probability to
> modify --- transformed parameters and model.
>
>> something like
>>
>> |
>> parameters {
>>   vector[K] z;
>> }
>> model {
>>   vector[K] s;
>>   s <- normalize2uniform(z);
>> }
>> |
>>
>> would be equivalent to
>>
>> |
>> parameters {
>>   vector[K] z;
>> }
>> model {
>>   vector[K] s;
>>   s <- z / sqrt(dot_self(z))
>>   z ~ normal(0.0, 1.0);
>> }
>
> I'm afraid I can't quite follow the intent of this
> transform.  What's going to happen with the s?
>
> But whatever it's intent, we could code the
> first thing so that it behaves like the second in just
> the way you suggest.
>
> I was thinking we'd transform something like:
>
>  parameters {
>    real mu;
>    real sigma;
>    real y;
>  }
>  model {
>    y ~ normal(mu,sigma);
>  }
>
> to be equivalent to this:
>
>  parameters {
>    real mu;
>    real sigma;
>    real y_unit;
>  }
>  transformed parameters {
>    real y;
>    y <- mu + sigma * y_unit;
>  }
>  model {
>    y_unit ~ normal(0,1);
>  }
>
> But that I'm not so sure how to do because it's not
> just adding a function, and it drops an implicit y_raw
> value on users.  And I believe there will be ordering
> issues that are complicated if there are multiple instances.
>
>> I guess either Stan would need to know that it needs to pass the log-posterior by value to functions like
>> normalize2uniform or we would have to rearrange the scope so that such functions could modify lp__ .
>
> I think you meant by non-constant reference rather than by
> value.  Most arguments are passed by constant reference.  All
> we have to do is drop the "const" in the definition and it can
> modify its inputs.  So far, I've tried to stay away from doing
> that explicitly because I think reference vs. value is a complicated
> enough concept that it'll confuse users.  Passing by const
> reference gives us the efficiency of pass by ref with the
> transparency of pass-by-value.
>
> - Bob
>

messages.subject: fixing print() & diagnostic_stream in command
messages.body_plain:
I'm trying to fix the broken print() command so that it
prints every iteration.  Stan 2.0.0 broke it.

Should print() print to the diagnostic_stream variable
in gm/command.hpp?

Or should it always print to std::cout?

As is, it's not printing anywhere.  There weren't enough
arguments being passed into the writers (the danger
of default values --- I'm thinking we should stop using
these whenerever we can get away with it because they've
caused us no end of trouble like this).

I just changed the command so that print() always
prints to std::cout, but that meant replacing some
uses of diagnostic_stream with &std::cout.  And I'm
not sure that's right.

There's a local variable "diagnostic_stream" in
command.hpp that's being set if a diagnostic file
is specified and left as 0 otherwise.

   1.   print() always prints to std::cout

   2.   print() prints to the diagnostic stream
        if a diagnostic_file is specified in the command

   3.   both of the above

We could also print to std::cerr, but that's tricky given
that std::cout and std::cerr aren't synched.

Then there's the issue of what to do for optimization.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
I would prefer diagnostic_stream not be muddied up with print
output, as it would make using the diagnostic_stream a pain --
at the moment diagnosic_stream is basically treated like a csv,
or whatever Stan format we define in the future.  If you were to
inject the print output it would have to at least be formatted as comments
(right now #, but again we don't really have an output spec) to
avoid breaking the current uses of the stream.  Another concern
is the size of the resulting diagnostic_stream which would grow
rapidly.

OK.

We can do what Boost static config does and actually define
the functions with no arguments, just the types (which you
need to resolve which function is called).  In a typical
templated function for us, that'd look like this:

     template <typename T1, ..., typename TN>
     inline
     typename promote_args<T1,...,TN>::type
     foo(const typename promote_args<T1,...,TN>::type& /* ignore lp arg */,
         int src_line,

         ... other args ...) {

          ... do something ...

          ... if something goes wrong, report source position ...
     }

We could make the source_line a size_t type and we could also
include a source column.

This is a pretty big change, but we can tackle it function by function
if we get the right conventions into place.

Both the testing and the passing of source and the deterrent to
inlining by making the functions bigger and more conditional will
potentially cause a noticeable slowdown.

So if we still want to have a way of turning the error checking
off, that's much trickier.  Then we have to dummy out the source_line
arg with an ifdef along with the tests.

- Bob

messages.subject: random number generation tweaks in
messages.body_plain:
Before I file an issue, I want to make sure I'm not
just missing the way to specify the chain ID.

We used that in Stan 1.3 in order to discard a number
of draws from the RNG.  It's efficient in Boost using
the discard() method in RNGs like

   http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_55_0/doc/html/boost/random/additive_combine_engine.html

The question is whether to make the Stan command line
specify the number to discard

    ./my-model ... random seed=123 discard=10000000000

or to make it something more like we have before, which
I'm not sure how to name.  If we want to imply that we're
using it to run parallel RNGs from the same initial seed,
we could go with something like:

    ./my-model ... random seed=123 parallel=2

to do the same thing as our --chain=2 used to do.

With all this fancy argument apparatus, we could also think
about making discard only apply to some RNGs.  Or we could
implement parallel differently for different RNGs.

RNGs have not been a problem for us before, so making
them configurable (beyond being able to discard) is not
at all a high priority.

Ben's been talking about replacing what we have with a newer
L'Ecuyer RNG, but I'd say if we do that, we just go with that
one and not make everything super-configurable for RNG.

- Bob

What if we just provide the transform and Jacobian determinant functions as normal functions?  E.G.,  allow users to write

parameters {
  vector[N] z;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[N] positive_z;

  positive_z <- exp_transform(z);
  increment_log_prob(exp_transform_lpcorrection(z));
}

This way exp_transform() and exp_transform_lpcorrection() are just normal functions.

Alternatively, maybe we use a different operator for this?  Maybe =  E.G.,

transformed parameters {
  vector[N] positive_z;

  positive_z = exp_transform(z);
}

Which then implicitly includes the increment_log_prob(exp_transform_lpcorrection(z)) line?

The nice side-effect of this notation (or any other similar one) is, when we can do higher order autodiff or symbolic differentiation, we could use this for more general transforms and then automatically compute the Jacobian of the transform.

>         int src_line,

>

> include a source column.
>
> This is a pretty big change, but we can tackle it function by function
> if we get the right conventions into place.
>
> Both the testing and the passing of source and the deterrent to
> inlining by making the functions bigger and more conditional will
> potentially cause a noticeable slowdown.
>
> So if we still want to have a way of turning the error checking
> off, that's much trickier.  Then we have to dummy out the source_line
> arg with an ifdef along with the tests.

What if we do what we've done with some of the transformation code: add try{}catch{} blocks to the generated code which catches exceptions, prepends a message with the the source line number and rethrows it.  Or, if we wanted to avoid many individual try{}catch{} blocks we could do something like:

int source_line_number = 0;
try {
  source_line_number = 1;
  ... do line 1 stuff ...

  source_line_number = 4;
  ... do line 4 stuff ...
}
catch () {
  ... report catching exception that was generated on line number source_line_number....
}

This might be a bit cleaner.  In either case, if we wanted to be really fancy, it would be nice if we could even print the model code along with it's line number.

I'd looked into doing something like this in the past, and the issue has always been getting the line numbers out of the parser and keeping them around when generating the code.  I'd never been able to penetrate the parser code enough to figure out how to do it.

Cheers,
Marcus

> >      >     We can come up with another kind of convention or instead
> >      >     make a list and keep it in a set-like data structure.
> >      >
> >      >
> >      > That might be better.
> >      >
> >      >
> >      > What if we just provide the transform and Jacobian determinant functions as normal functions?  E.G.,  allow users
> >     to write
> >      >
> >      > parameters {
> >      >   vector[N] z;
> >      > }
> >      > transformed parameters {
> >      >   vector[N] positive_z;
> >      >
> >      >   positive_z <- exp_transform(z);
> >      >   increment_log_prob(exp_transform_lpcorrection(z));
> >      > }
> >      >
> >      > This way exp_transform() and exp_transform_lpcorrection() are just normal functions.
> >      >
> >      > Alternatively, maybe we use a different operator for this?  Maybe =  E.G.,
> >      >
> >      > transformed parameters {
> >      >   vector[N] positive_z;
> >      >
> >      >   positive_z = exp_transform(z);
> >      > }
> >      >
> >      > Which then implicitly includes the increment_log_prob(exp_transform_lpcorrection(z)) line?
> >      >
> >      >
> >      > The nice side-effect of this notation (or any other similar one) is, when we can do higher order autodiff or
> >     symbolic differentiation, we could use this for more general transforms and then automatically compute the Jacobian
> >     of the transform.
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >
> >      >     We're also going to have to think about better error reporting
> >      >     for functions like sqrt() that are in the lib.  If we want to pass
> >      >     in code location for debugging to all of our calls, then we could
> >      >     also just always pass in lp__ as the last arg.
> >      >
> >      >
> >      > Always pass it in but for most functions make it a const reference? I guess that could work but it seems like there
> >      > should be a better way.
> >      >
> >      > We can do what Boost static config does and actually define
> >      > the functions with no arguments, just the types (which you
> >      > need to resolve which function is called).  In a typical
> >      > templated function for us, that'd look like this:
> >      >
> >      >     template <typename T1, ..., typename TN>
> >      >     inline
> >      >     typename promote_args<T1,...,TN>::type
> >      >     foo(const typename promote_args<T1,...,TN>::type& /* ignore lp arg */,
> >      >         int src_line,
> >      >
> >      >         ... other args ...) {
> >      >
> >      >          ... do something ...
> >      >
> >      >          ... if something goes wrong, report source position ...
> >      >     }
> >      >
> >      > We could make the source_line a size_t type and we could also
> >      > include a source column.
> >      >
> >      > This is a pretty big change, but we can tackle it function by function
> >      > if we get the right conventions into place.
> >      >
> >      > Both the testing and the passing of source and the deterrent to
> >      > inlining by making the functions bigger and more conditional will
> >      > potentially cause a noticeable slowdown.
> >      >
> >      > So if we still want to have a way of turning the error checking
> >      > off, that's much trickier.  Then we have to dummy out the source_line
> >      > arg with an ifdef along with the tests.
> >      >
> >      >
> >      > What if we do what we've done with some of the transformation code: add try{}catch{} blocks to the generated code
> >     which catches exceptions, prepends a message with the the source line number and rethrows it.  Or, if we wanted to
> >     avoid many individual try{}catch{} blocks we could do something like:
> >      >
> >      > int source_line_number = 0;
> >      > try {
> >      >   source_line_number = 1;
> >      >   ... do line 1 stuff ...
> >      >
> >      >   source_line_number = 4;
> >      >   ... do line 4 stuff ...
> >      > }
> >      > catch () {
> >      >   ... report catching exception that was generated on line number source_line_number....
> >      > }
> >      >
> >      > This might be a bit cleaner.  In either case, if we wanted to be really fancy, it would be nice if we could even
> >     print the model code along with it's line number.
> >      >
> >      > I'd looked into doing something like this in the past, and the issue has always been getting the line numbers out
> >     of the parser and keeping them around when generating the code.  I'd never been able to penetrate the parser code
> >     enough to figure out how to do it.
> >      >
> >      > Cheers,
> >      > Marcus

On Monday, November 18, 2013 12:22:02 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Ben's been talking about replacing what we have with a newer
> L'Ecuyer RNG, but I'd say if we do that, we just go with that
> one and not make everything super-configurable for RNG.

I don't know that user configuration is a huge priority, because the idea of parallel PRNG is so complicated that I wouldn't expect most users to know what to do (and those that do know what to do can change the source locally). That said, it seems like the Boost-compatible parallel PRNGs all have an abstract class that they inherit from, so if you figure out how to use one, you can basically use any of them.

I am pretty sure no one affirmatively recommends the PRNG Stan currently uses. It is like 25 years old. I think the most widely regarded library is

http://numbercrunch.de/trng/

but someone from DE Shaw argued for the inclusion of another one on the Boost mailing list

http://lists.boost.org/Archives/boost/2012/01/189293.php

Ben

messages.body_snippet:

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sd() problem: sqrt(square(0))
messages.body_plain:
I can fix it.  I worked out the analytic gradients,
which don't have this problem.  That'll solve the
specific case of sd().

Not much we can do about general code that does sqrt(0)
but has some analytic reduction, like sqrt(square(x)) = x.
In general, there are lots of ways to express square(x), such
as x * x.  And the  case for sd() is more like sqrt(sum(square(x)).

I don't know how to do runtime type resolution, but we
might be able to catch the expression tree structure and
collapse it.   But that doesn't solve the multiple ways
to express it problem.

- Bob

On 11/19/13, 4:38 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> We're getting nan's in sd() when all the elements are the same.
>
> It's really coming from taking the sqrt of the square of 0. A minimal test case:
>
>     #include <stan/agrad/rev/sqrt.hpp>
>     #include <gtest/gtest.h>
>     #include <stan/agrad/var.hpp>
>
>     TEST(AgradRev,sqrt_square_zero) {
>        stan::agrad::var x(0.0);
>        stan::agrad::var f = sqrt(square(x));
>
>        EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(0.0,f.val());
>        std::vector<stan::agrad::var> g;
>        g.push_back(x);
>        std::vector<double> gradient;
>        f.grad(g,gradient);
>        EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(1.0,gradient[0]);
>     }
>
>
> The gradient ends up being nan. By the way, this happens with multiplying x by itself as well. And if we change the
> function order.
>
> The two chain methods (just the relevant pieces pulled out):
>
> sqrt:
>          void chain() {
>            avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * val_);
>          }
>
> square:
>          void chain() {
>            avi_->adj_ += adj_ * 2.0 * avi_->val_;
>          }
>
>
> In the test case outlined above, we start with the chain method in sqrt with:
> avi_->adj_ = 0
> adj_ = 1
> avi_->val_ = inf
> The resulting adjoint value is as expected: inf. (this seems reasonable in the limit as x approaches 0.)
>
> Then we apply the chain rule and get into the chain method in sqrt with:
> avi_->adj_ = 0
> adj_ = inf
> avi_->val_ = 0
> The resulting adjoint value blows up: nan. This is from the inf * 2 * 0 condition. inf * 0 = nan.
>
> The obvious right answer is d/dx sqrt(square(x)) = d/dx x = 1, but I can't figure out how to get there from local chain
> functions without some knowledge of the expression tree. An inf or 0 could arise in lots of ways, so it doesn't seem
> like creating a special case is the right thing to do.
>
> So... what should we do?
>
>
> Daniel
>
>

messages.body_plain:
Didn't this issue come up a while back?

Mathematically, the derivative d/dx (sqrt(x)) is not well defined at x=0 so in some sense we can put whatever value we want because basically everything is wrong.  From a functional perspective, we never want to get a non-finite gradient out of the autodiff unless we absolutely must (e.g., someone divides by zero).  Putting those two things together, maybe we can just rewrite chain for sqrt() to be:

        void chain() {
          if (val_ > 1e-300)

              avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * val_);

          else
              avi_->adj_ += adj_ / 2.0;
        }

or, alternatively,

        void chain() {
          avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * std::max(val_,2e-300));
        }

Cheers,
Marcus

>
> Yes. I was trying to reduce it to the simplest case.
>
> > I don't know how to do runtime type resolution, but we
> > might be able to catch the expression tree structure and

> > to express it problem.
>
> Hmmm.

> > On 11/19/13, 4:38 PM, Daniel Lee wrote:
> > > We're getting nan's in sd() when all the elements are the same.
> > >
> > > It's really coming from taking the sqrt of the square of 0. A minimal test case:
> > >
> > >     #include <stan/agrad/rev/sqrt.hpp>
> > >     #include <gtest/gtest.h>
> > >     #include <stan/agrad/var.hpp>
> > >
> > >     TEST(AgradRev,sqrt_square_zero) {
> > >        stan::agrad::var x(0.0);
> > >        stan::agrad::var f = sqrt(square(x));
> > >
> > >        EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(0.0,f.val());
> > >        std::vector<stan::agrad::var> g;
> > >        g.push_back(x);
> > >        std::vector<double> gradient;
> > >        f.grad(g,gradient);
> > >        EXPECT_FLOAT_EQ(1.0,gradient[0]);
> > >     }
> > >
> > >
> > > The gradient ends up being nan. By the way, this happens with multiplying x by itself as well. And if we change the
> > > function order.
> > >
> > > The two chain methods (just the relevant pieces pulled out):
> > >
> > > sqrt:
> > >          void chain() {
> > >            avi_->adj_ += adj_ / (2.0 * val_);
> > >          }
> > >
> > > square:
> > >          void chain() {

> > >          }
> > >

> > > In the test case outlined above, we start with the chain method in sqrt with:
> > > avi_->adj_ = 0
> > > adj_ = 1
> > > avi_->val_ = inf
> > > The resulting adjoint value is as expected: inf. (this seems reasonable in the limit as x approaches 0.)
> > >
> > > Then we apply the chain rule and get into the chain method in sqrt with:
> > > avi_->adj_ = 0
> > > adj_ = inf
> > > avi_->val_ = 0
> > > The resulting adjoint value blows up: nan. This is from the inf * 2 * 0 condition. inf * 0 = nan.

OK, is it OK with everyone to throw an exception?
Basically, returning NaN is tantamount to doing just
that in the context of Stan's log prob and gradient
evals.

We do the same thing with abs(x) itself, taking its
derivative to be 0 at 0.  This seems more sensible than for
sqrt, as the limit from the left is -1 and from the right is 1.

There's a big problem with inits of 0, which can
inadvertently land you right on one of these discontinuities.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] sd() problem: sqrt(square(0))
messages.body_plain:
Returning a subgradient won't affect HMC at all except maybe on the level of efficiency but then only when there is significant mass at that region and even then I expect the impact to be small because we're returning something which will be close.  It's not "bad statistical mojo" as It certainly won't impact the statistical validity of our samples since a) the Metropolis test will use the same "correct" log prob and b) so long as the same subgradient is returned, the simulation will be reversible.  Patching the gradient is basically just using a different simulation Hamiltonian which is only different from the correct one in a small region around these gradient singularities.

If we throw an exception we're just going to reject everything and stop sampling in that region altogether.   Further, these rejections won't just occur at exactly x = 0, returning an unusually large gradient can overflow chain() calculations elsewhere resulting in a nan or inf gradient.

Regarding efficiency of patching the gradient vs throwing an exception, it's not clear which will be more efficient.  It seems to me allowing it to traverse through a region instead of automatically rejecting any trajectory which comes near the singularity would be more statistically efficient.

messages.subject: BibTeX and links for papers on web site
messages.subject_clean: BibTeX and links for papers on web site
messages.body_plain:
Michael and I have had a whack at redesigning the
web site.   The latest version is in the repo
webpages under mc-stan.org/index.html <http://mc-stan.org/index.html>.

Right now, we have BibTeX for the papers.

Two questions:

1.  move to just a bibliography-style citation and
     don't be so complete, and

2.  include links?

We'll keep the BibTeX for the links we suggest for
referring to Stan.

Pro and con for 1 are obvious.

Pro for 2 is that it's more incentive to actually look
at the papers.  Con is that links rot and are harder to
include in the first place.

My own experience trying to do this over two decades is
that links always rot.  Things are much better now than 10
years ago.  Responsible sites will redirect, but journals
get sold, consolidated, move to JSTOR, etc.  (This was
part of the motivation for the DOI system, but it hasn't
been widely accepted outside of bio.)

The question to me is whether the live links make up for
us having to create them, and then either check them or
let them go dead.

- Bob

On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 12:12 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 11:52 AM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Returning a subgradient won't affect HMC at all except maybe on the level of efficiency but then only when there is significant mass at that region and even then I expect the impact to be small because we're returning something which will be close.
>
> Unfortunately, we're artificially giving mass in these regions significant mass since we're initializing starting at 0.

That doesn't give the region mass.  If it has little real mass, sampling should quickly transition out of the region assuming that sampling can actually proceed.

>
> > It's not "bad statistical mojo" as It certainly won't impact the statistical validity of our samples since a) the Metropolis test will use the same "correct" log prob and b) so long as the same subgradient is returned, the simulation will be reversible.  Patching the gradient is basically just using a different simulation Hamiltonian which is only different from the correct one in a small region around these gradient singularities.
> >
> > If we throw an exception we're just going to reject everything and stop sampling in that region altogether.   Further, these rejections won't just occur at exactly x = 0, returning an unusually large gradient can overflow chain() calculations elsewhere resulting in a nan or inf gradient.
> >
> > Regarding efficiency of patching the gradient vs throwing an exception, it's not clear which will be more efficient.  It seems to me allowing it to traverse through a region instead of automatically rejecting any trajectory which comes near the singularity would be more statistically efficient.
>
> I'm in favor of catching errors early. One reason this was difficult to track down from the outside was due to the gradients going to nan without informative error messages. It was baffling because it only happened with sampling and not with optimization or test gradient mode. I believe we'll get a handle on the sqrt(square(0)) case soon, but the fundamental reason for this issue isn't going away and I'd like to be able to identify the problems much quicker.

Catching errors early is good but throwing exceptions is only useful if the caller is actually in a position to do something useful about it or there is no other resory.  In this case, all the caller can do is reject the sample and/or bail back to the user who is even less equipped to do something about it.

> Right now, I don't think we check gradients for nan values. Should we? It seems like a reasonable thing to do as opposed to what we currently do now, which is to integrate using nan derivatives and failing when the nans propagate to the positions. This could be done independent of error checking using exceptions.

We should definitely be checking gradients for non-finite values.

Cheers,
Marcus

On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 12:38 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> I thought a NaN gradient would throw the same exception that bad constraints does
> but I guess I'm wrong.  We could just have the gradient functors check and throw
> the necessary exceptions.

No, the checks on probability distributions only check the values, not adjoints. And the basic math functions don't have the same checks. We behave like the standard template library and default to their behavior on taking in nans, infs, 0s, and other boundary conditions where reasonable.

messages.body_plain:
There are two options -- either there's not enough mass around zero, chains never hit the singularity, and everything is fine.  But if there is enough mass around zero then the chains can hit the singularity and problems arise.  As Dan noted the fact that people like "0" makes initialization a problem even if sampling isn't.  In either case, the user should be informed because they have an ill-defined gradient being used in their model which is a bad idea™ as it is usually indicative of a modeling (or initialization) mistake.

messages.body_plain:
On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 12:54 PM, Daniel Lee <bea...@alum.mit.edu> wrote:
> On Wed, Nov 20, 2013 at 12:48 PM, Marcus Brubaker <marcus.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > If we change the gradient near singularities does it still get stuck?
>
> No, it moves and samples just fine.
>
> >  Throwing an exception effectively punts the problem to the user.  I agree that we should be producing better error better error messages.
>
> Yes, exactly. It's going to be difficult to hunt down every singular point. If users are alerted to a problem, if it's an actual problem with Stan code, I'm trusting that enough people will bring it to our attention. So yes, punting the problem to the user seems like the right thing to do.

But what's our response once it's been brought to our attention?  Should we work around it by patching gradients where reasonable?

Anyway, just to put a clear plan out there for us to discuss:

1) We should be checking gradients for non-finite values and reporting this as an error as soon as it's reasonable to detect.
2) Reporting more detailed error messages would be nice if we can find a way to do it without killing performance.  Perhaps we could have a compile-time option to check all adjoints after every individual chain() call.  This will be expensive, but will tell us precisely where our gradients go awry.  Alternatively we could add code to every chain() function but that's probably more work than simply hunting down every singular point.
3) When such errors are found and reported I think we should patch the gradients where it's reasonable to do so.  If the function itself is well defined at a point, we can generally come up with a reasonable subgradient which will allow sampling to proceed instead of simply punting the problem up the chain where there is less ability to do anything productive about it.

Basically all of the unconstrained parameters have been defined so that 0 inits should provide a reasonable starting point.  If a reasonable model (e.g., the double exponential) cannot be initialized at zero that seems like something we should fix as opposed to just saying it's a modelling mistake or requiring our users to jump through the massive hoops required for an explicit manual initialization.  I think this would be a somewhat different discussion if we had manual initialization block so we could just tell the user "change your initialization for this variable".

Cheers,
Marcus

I think this boils down to what we'd like to
see happen for the following calculation where
x and y are parameters:

   mean <- (x + y) / 2;

The problem is that the current auto-diff's brute-force application
of the chain rule is going to kill the code on the sqrt(0)
if x == y.

We can write our own sd() with analytic gradients and solve
the problem for that case.

But the real issue is what to do for the above model?

in RStan more heavily.

messages.subject: definition of "variance"
messages.body_plain:
[pulled into its own thread for semantics mavens]

On 11/20/13, 1:50 PM, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> Hi, I'm confused.  Var should divide by n-1, not by n.
> I'm not joking here, dividing by n-1 is the definition.

Sorry --- bad example.  Stan absolutely divides by N-1
in the sd() and var() functions.

I'd go even further and separate four concepts that are
often just called "variance" in the literature:

   1.  variance (of a random variable or distribution)

   2.  population variance

   3.  sample variance

   4.  estimate of variance based on a sample

For (1), everyone divides by N for finite discrete random variables

For (2), Snedecor and Cochran (closest reliable book at hand) define
population variance as dividing by N.

For (3), Snedecor and Cochran define sample variance as dividing by N-1.

For (4), we know there are many estimators, the MLE (divide by N)
and unbiased (divide by N-1) being the usual pair in intro math
stats books.  Arguably, a point estimate of variance should not
be called "variance", no matter how you define it.

Yet one more reason intro stat students (like I was only very very
recently and arguably still am) get really
really really confused from the standard presentations of this
material in intro courses and books and tutorials.  For instance,
the R doc, always a source of enlightment, says simply:

   This function computes the standard deviation of the values in x.

and later in the details section:

   Like var this uses denominator n - 1.

   The standard deviation of a zero-length vector (after removal of
   NAs if na.rm = TRUE) is not defined and gives an error. The standard deviation
   of a length-one vector is NA.

> We can have the convention that if n=1, we define variance to be 0.

We return the special NaN value rather than returning 0.  We
treat it as 0 in n_eff calcs, though, I believe, so we don't get
all those NaN cases when a param doesn't move in a chain.

- Bob

messages.subject: boundary conditions of sd() + doc
messages.body_plain:
Sorry --- I keep confusing the 0 and 1 cases.
If size(x) == 0, then we raise an error.  We could
have this case also return 0 and thus deal with the boundary
condition of empty bins in models.

In Stan 2.0.1, if size(x) == 1, then

    sd(x) = var(x) = 0

and

   d/dx_1 sd(x) = d/dx_1 var(x) = 0

Whatever we decide, I'll improve the doc in the manual to reflect
the boundary cases.  We really need to do this for all of our functions,
as it's coming up a lot in user models.  So expect about five
dozen of these discussions for everything from trig to Bessel
functions :-)

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: scare quotes, air quotes, and sketchy terminology
messages.body_plain:
On 11/21/13, 10:41 AM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
...

> Merged.  I will defend those italics to the death!  I mean, I'm pretty sure they're reasonable style.

In this particular case, I think the quotes around "fast" and "slow"
signal that you haven't quite come up with the right terminology.
Instead, you're adapting some commonly used words to do slightly different
work.  If that's not what you intended to signal, then the usage is wrong.

Here's an excellent summary of this kind of quote usage:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation_mark#Signaling_unusual_usage

I'm with the U Chicago Manual of Style on this one.

The unusual usage application comes very close to what are commonly
called "scare quotes":

   http://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/scare_quote

So just imagine yourself making air quotes every time you use them
and you should be OK.

- Bob

P.S.  All of the quotes in this email signal mentions of words, not uses
of words:

   http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quotation_mark#Use.E2.80.93mention_distinction

P.P.S.  Next week on the grammar channel, we'll pit "Markov chain Monte Carlo"
and "no-U-turn sampler" against "Markov Chain Monte Carlo" and
"No-U-Turn Sampler".

that you generated the results using a recreatable hash
tag in GitHub.  I can respect that commitment to reproducibility.

clutter in the form of Stan branches that are no longer under
development.

into develop and you can tag that.  Develop and its history will persist,
at least while we're on GitHub.

Long term, you may be better off just making a tarball that's
under your control.  I think we'll be able to keep the tarballs
(now zipballs) for official releases, but it's going to be
a few days before we can even get 2.0.2 out, and that sounds like
it's going to be too late for your schedule even if we do commit
to releasing a 2.1.0 with your pull request instead of a simpler
2.0.2 patch release.  There's the issue of RStan and PyStan catching
up, too, but there's no reason we can't release Stan version N before
RStan or PyStan version N.

On 11/21/13, 3:20 PM, Michael Betancourt wrote:
 > They're italics, as in emphasizing a word when it is first introduced.  That falls into the common
 > convention of many styles.

This is all just FYI -- if we were going to get super
picky about manual style and grammar we'd need a better
copy editor than me!

For instance, compare and contrast these:

    We define "variance" to be the average squared distance from the mean.

    Variance is the average squared distance from the mean.

The first should be quoted, because it's a mention of
the term.  The second should not be quoted, because it's
a use of the word.  The second usage is sometimes italicized
in technical books to highlight definitions.

Now we're ready for some philosophy.  The sentence

   "Red" means red.

not only makes sense, but is not a tautology.  The first
instance is a mention, the second a use.  Compare and contrast
with

   "Rouge" means red.

- Bob

management again, which we should reserve for the next Stan meeting.

to denote a casual definition - something used for notational
convenience but shouldn't be taken too seriously.  I'm fine with
defining a consistent Stan style but let's be careful about differentiating
a consistent style from a "correct" style.  Damn straight I used quotes.

> picky about manual style and grammar we'd need a better
> copy editor than me!
>
> For instance, compare and contrast these:
>
>   We define "variance" to be the average squared distance from the mean.
>
>   Variance is the average squared distance from the mean.
>
> The first should be quoted, because it's a mention of
> the term.  The second should not be quoted, because it's
> a use of the word.  The second usage is sometimes italicized
> in technical books to highlight definitions.

messages.subject: Re: Remaining work for v2.0.2
messages.body_plain:
One thing we should probably add to the release process is to reformat the code consistently. There is a clang tool for this, although we would need to write a set of rules to enforce Bob style (by default it only knows LLVM, Google, Chromium, Mozilla, and Webkit styles).

http://clang.llvm.org/docs/ClangFormat.html

With LLVM style, it is just

find src/ -type f -name \*\.\[ch]pp -print | xargs -n 1 -P 9 clang-format-3.4 --style=LLVM -i

which results in a diff that is 270948 lines long.

Ben

P.S. Also, src/test/mcmc/mock_hmc.hpp has a recently messed-up header guard. Somebody put that fix on top of an existing pull-request; it is not worth running the whole set of tests just for something like that.

messages.subject: code (re)formatting
messages.body_plain:
On 11/22/13, 9:37 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> One thing we should probably add to the release process is to reformat the code consistently. There is a clang tool for
> this, although we would need to write a set of rules to enforce Bob style (by default it only knows LLVM, Google,
> Chromium, Mozilla, and Webkit styles).

I don't have a problem with a loose guide and not being
too picky about it.  For me, it's just about keeping the
code readable.

 From first principles, I'd say go with Kernighan, Ritchie,
and Stroustroup.   I said that before looking it up.  Turns
out they use the style I like for conditionals and for loops
(space before the open round parens, open curly on same line),
and the style Mike likes for functions (open curlies on their
own line).

If we automate, won't it mess up all the outstanding pull
requests?  I'm curious how well the Clang tool works.  I've
never seen one work very well, but they'll have the parser
sorted, which is the hardest part.

- Bob
